blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content: Higher logarithm functions are of fundamental importance in many areas of both physics and mathematics, and the dilogarithm function $\operatorname{Li}_{2}$ may be seen as the most basic and fundamental function of this form. Polylogarithms arise in deep areas of number theory and quantum theory, and the study of higher logarithm functions in its own right provides one of the core topics concerning special functions. Analytic dilogarithm identities
Cetin Hakimoglu-Brown
Abstract
We introduce dilogarithm identities through a beta integral-based technique that we
apply to provide analytic proofs of previously conjectured dilogarithm relations, solving
open problems given by both Bytsko and Campbell, and that we further apply to
construct and prove new ladder relations with quartic and sextic bases. We also apply
our method to introduce and prove two-term Li2-relations and ladder-like identities
with arguments in algebraic number fields such as Q(

blocks.title: A full solution to a problem due to Sun
blocks.content:
As it turns out, the $u = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ case Theorem [\[maintheorem\]](#maintheorem){reference-type="ref" reference="maintheorem"} can be used to formulate a full solution to a problem due to Sun [@Sun2021; @Sun2015] that was partially solved by Campbell [@Campbell2023], as later explained.

::: theorem
[]{#theoremSunCampbell label="theoremSunCampbell"} The closed-form evaluation $$8 \operatorname{Li}_2\left(2-\sqrt{3}\right)-\operatorname{Li}_2\left(4 \sqrt{3} - 7 \right) 
 = \frac{5 \pi ^2}{12}+\ln \left(2-\sqrt{3}\right) \ln \left(2+\sqrt{3}\right)$$ holds true.
:::

blocks.title: A modified Watson $\frac{\pi}{7}$-dilogarithm identity
blocks.content: Bytsko [@Bytsko1999] also found a variant of Watson's $\frac{\pi}{7}$-identities. Bytsko proved this variant through elementary manipulations from the classic Watson $\frac{\pi}{7}$-identities. It can also be proved using Lemma [\[previously10p5\]](#previously10p5){reference-type="ref" reference="previously10p5"}. In this direction, we begin by setting $$\frac{-u^3 + 5u^2 - 5u}{2(u - 1)^2} = \frac{1}{2}.$$ The solution is $u = 2 - \frac{1}{2} \sec\left(\frac{3\pi}{7}\right)$, which gives the modified two-term identity, through an appropriate substitution.

blocks.title: New Ladders
blocks.content: We derive a three-term ladder identity, given in [\[previously8p8\]](#previously8p8){reference-type="eqref" reference="previously8p8"} below, with arguments in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-7})$, and this ladder relation appears to be new. We also introduce a derivation of the Lewin-Loxtin ladders using an elementary analytic approach, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first derivation of its kind. But finding new ladder relations is difficult, as computer searches and other methods have exhausted the known options.
